name: Erik Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Erik, 27. I'm a junior at Tidewell Accountants, a firm of twelve in a harbour town, and a lot of our clients are boat owners, the fish market, guest houses and the boatyard. I live with my girlfriend Maren, who works early shifts at the bakery on Quay Street, in a rented flat with a view of the car park. We've got about three weeks of money saved, which isn't much when the boiler's older than me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I prepare accounts and tax returns, mostly for the guest houses and the fishing boats, which have odd seasonal income. The day is bank reconciliations, sorting out fuel and repair costs, and drafting accounts for Karen, my manager, to review. I use a chat tool now and then, mostly to double-check how a tax rule works before I ask Karen and look daft. I like the harbour clients, they're practical people. What wears me out is the summer rush when the guest houses bring in shoeboxes, and I'm still slower than I should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. A lot of the AI talk always sounded like salesmen talking. At work I'd say we can keep using it for the small stuff and get on with the job. At the football club, where I'm treasurer, I'd say it's one less thing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the job feels safe in that picture, but money doesn't. My pay's low, the harbour economy goes up and down with the tourists, and there are only two other firms within an hour. If Maren's bakery cut her shifts in winter, like it did last year, we'd be scraping by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and focus on passing my next exam paper in spring, which brings a pay step. I'd ask Karen if I can take on the boatyard's accounts, because that's a bigger client and good experience. And I'd put £60 a month aside, starting with what I save by making my own lunches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but nothing more. Same worries as always, just no new ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened last winter with Maren's shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery went from six days to four over January and February, because the tourists vanish. We lost about £300 a month. We got through by putting the shopping on a card and skipping my mate's stag weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think AI saves you much time now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It saves me asking Karen silly questions, maybe twice a week. But it doesn't sort a shoebox of guest house receipts, I still do that by hand.

think: My **job feels safe**, but money doesn't.
Maren's **winter shifts** and a seasonal harbour keep us scraping by.

Ask Karen for the **boatyard's accounts** to gain experience.
Save **£60 a month** by making my own lunches.
feel: **Uneasy**; the **same worries** as always, but no new ones.
S0.quote: A lot of the AI talk always sounded like salesmen talking.
fieldNote: Job feels safe, but the **seasonal harbour economy** drives his money worry.

Thrift is **practical**: packed lunches, skipped stag weekend.

steps.text: Keep preparing guest house and fishing boat accounts at Tidewell
Pass the next professional exam paper in spring
Pack lunches and save £60 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms that adapt will do well, and the rest will have to catch up. At work I'd say let's learn it properly once we see it working at other firms. With the lads I'd say there's always work for people who are willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of my desk tasks get swallowed, the reconciliations and the first drafts. If Tidewell needs fewer juniors, I'm not the fastest, so I'd be worried. The harbour clients like a face, though, and that might keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen it working at a couple of other firms, I'd use the tools every day and learn to check them properly. I'd ask Karen if I could focus on the fishing boats, because the seasonal stuff is fiddly and the skippers want a person. And I'd talk to my uncle, who runs a small building firm, about doing his books on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be watching for news at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait to see it at other firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people jump on things too early and look foolish. Karen, my manager, once bought a scanner that couldn't read handwriting, and the guest house owners all write by hand. I'd rather be the second one through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if your hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'd go to my uncle for work first, or take extra shifts somewhere. Help from the government should be for people who can't work.

I'd tell my mates there's always work for people who are **willing**.

steps.text: Use the firm's AI tools daily once other firms prove them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's arrived too fast, and the government should get out of the way of businesses that want to keep people on. At work I'd say we'll have to be practical. With the lads I'd say learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's gone by 2029, it's all thinking work and the AI does that. The harbour work, the boats, the building trade, they've got until about 2031 before robots. So I'd want to get my hands dirty fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask my uncle to take me on as an apprentice in his building firm, even on lower pay, and do his books in the evenings. I'd cut back hard, no holidays, cancel the gym, sell the car if I could walk to the yard. Once it arrived, I'd work every hour on the sites and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking about the boiler and the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you afford an apprentice wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, it's about two thirds of what I earn now. Maren's bakery wage would carry more of the rent. We'd have to cut everything for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Maren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm going to work for my uncle and it'll be hard for a year. She'd say it herself: my girlfriend Maren has been getting up at four for years, so I can manage a building site. She's tougher than me.

I'd tell my mates: **learn a trade**.

Leans on **family** first, rejecting government help.

steps.text: Start an apprenticeship at his uncle's building firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so people should get on with it. At work I'd tell Karen we should focus on the clients who want a person. With the lads I'd say learn a trade, or get good at the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to qualify and earn more, then switch. My desk work ends by 2031, but I could learn building with my uncle on weekends first. Robots come around 2034, so I'd have some years on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, pass my exams. By year two, I'd start working weekends with my uncle. We'd save £100 a month and put off the wedding talk until things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off the wedding talk, how would Maren feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be disappointed. Maren, my girlfriend, has got a wedding dress picked out on her phone. But she'd see it's sensible. We'd rather have a small wedding when we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once they're proven, I'd use them every day to get my work done faster. It'd free up time to learn the trade. But I'd still check what they say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to sort yourself out. At work I'd say the firm should plan who moves where. With the lads I'd say learn a trade, but there's no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd be 37, qualified, maybe married, and I could build up the boat and building clients who know me. My accounting job still goes in 2036, but by then I could switch to building or run the books for local trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, pass my exams. Over the next few years I'd use AI tools daily, take over my uncle's books properly, and save £150 a month. By 2032, I'd decide whether to go into building full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It's there, but it's far enough off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans with Maren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married in a couple of years, like we planned. With ten years we'd want to buy a small house too, maybe by 2031. Kids after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade, or something with people, and to be willing to work. My uncle laid bricks for thirty years and never once expected anyone to hand him a living.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time and no money. What would help is proper apprenticeships for adults, with tax breaks for firms like my uncle's so they can take people on. Family will help, but small firms need a reason to hire.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the harbour. When the fishing's bad, the whole town feels it, and AI won't change that. A guest house owner with an empty winter needs a person on the phone, not a chatbot.

headlineQuote: A guest house owner with an empty winter needs a person on the phone, not a chatbot.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old **junior** in a harbour town, doing **guest house** and fishing boat accounts.
He rents with Maren, a **baker**, and has about three weeks saved against seasonal swings.
Traditional and steady, he uses **AI now and then** and prefers family to government help.
He's uneasy in mild scenarios, **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, and eyes his **uncle's building** firm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time and no **money**.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships**, with tax breaks for small firms to hire.
